name: mrcache
workload: GET of a single small value (16 B) and of a 10 kB value on one node over TCP, in-memory; README tables show ops/sec for mrcache, Redis and memcached, with the client harness bench/bench.go (Go, default 16 connections, 2 s, batch 1, one repeated key) in the repo but the README not stating which settings produced the tables.
claimed_speedup: README table 'GET - 16B (ops/sec)': mrcache 18.6m, redis 2.5m, memcached 400k (about 7.4x Redis and 46x memcached, derived from page data). 'GET - 10kb (ops/sec)': mrcache 979k, redis 313k, memcached 261k (about 3.1x and 3.8x, derived from page data); mrcache with zstd 212k is slower than both. README intro still says 'a key value cache with support for compression that is 25x faster than memcached' (matches the older 9.8m vs 400k table, not the current one). Older README revisions (commit e33dfb6, 2024-04-21): 16B GET mrcache 9.8m, redis 2.7m, memcached 400k.
compiler_and_flags: Server: gcc -O3 (Makefile CFLAGS = -O3), Linux kernel 5.8+, liburing, zstd; io_uring configured with SQPOLL, SINGLE_ISSUER, multishot accept/recv and provided buffer ring. Benchmark client: Go (go run bench.go). Redis and memcached versions, build and configuration are not stated.
tradeoffs: Single-node in-memory cache with a proprietary binary protocol (get/set/getz/setz; set has no response) and its own clients (Python asyncio asyncmrcache), so it is not a drop-in replacement for Redis or memcached. Needs Linux 5.8+ io_uring. Keys limited to under 32 kB, values under 16 MB. The hash index (open addressing, about 14 B per item) is allocated once at startup and never grows or shrinks, so it must be sized up front. Eviction is FIFO by dropping the oldest 16 MB block, not LRU; README documents per-item overhead of about 18 B against 50-60 B for Redis and memcached. No data structures, clustering or persistence documented. Optional zstd compression (getz/setz) roughly cuts 10 kB GET throughput to 212k.
caveats: Tier C: first-party README numbers with no CPU model, core count, kernel version, Redis or memcached version, connection count, pipelining/batch size or run command stated. The bench/bench.go harness in the repo has defaults of 16 connections and batch 1 and issues GET on one single key (zero-filled key and value) over and over, so the hot path is one cache-resident entry and the result mostly measures the network loop, not the hash index. bench.go only speaks mrcache's binary protocol and Redis RESP; it has no memcached mode, and bench/py/mc.py, red.py and mrc.py are one-shot smoke scripts, so the harness behind the memcached numbers is not in the repo. Its client counts a reply complete after length*batch bytes, which fits mrcache's reply but not the longer Redis RESP reply. Numbers moved between README revisions: 1.07m vs redis 270k vs memcached 100k (commit cce89a1, 2024-02-28), 9.8m vs 2.7m vs 400k (2024-02-29 to 2024-04-21), 18.6m vs 2.5m vs 400k (from 2024-04-24, after the io_uring multishot rewrite); the 10 kB rows stayed the same across the rewrite, so they predate it. The headline '25x faster than memcached' is stale against the current table (18.6m/400k is about 46x). The server uses io_uring SQPOLL, which keeps a kernel polling thread busy on an extra core; Redis in its default configuration runs commands on one thread and memcached defaults to 4 worker threads, so per-core fairness is unstated. Single-node in-memory scope only; no networked or persistence comparison. The README is inconsistent on the kernel requirement (5.5+ in the intro, 5.8+ in Dependencies) and the HEAD Makefile still links -lmrloop although the README no longer lists mrloop as a dependency (mrloop.h was removed in 2024-05), so a build may need fixes. No third-party measurement found (one WebSearch query returned nothing about mrcache).
